chunks: Design an ESC. The question: Design an ESC.
Designing an ESC is a sequence of choices that start with what it must do. First list the requirements: motor, battery voltage, current, command interface and size.
Then pick an architecture, size the key parts (MOSFETs, shunt, capacitors), write the firmware, and test it carefully.
It is like designing a bridge. You do not start by choosing steel. You start by asking what load it must carry and how far it must span.
Then you choose the structure, calculate the size of each part, and test it before anyone drives on it.
The analogy has one gap: an ESC's "load" includes heat, so thermal checks are as important as electrical ones.
The architecture I would draw.
Power flows from the battery down through the bridge; BEC and gate supplies hang off the input rail; the MCU gets position (back-EMF) and current feedback and commands the gate driver.
Requirements: voltage, current, interface, size and cost the design must meet.
R ds(on) : a MOSFET's resistance when switched on, which sets how much heat it makes while conducting. Shunt: a tiny resistor used to measure current.
Dead-time: a short pause so the two switches on one motor wire are never on at once.
Bootstrap: a capacitor circuit that gives the upper switches the extra voltage they need to turn on.
Say the target is a 4S LiPo battery (four lithium cells in series, 16. 8 volts when full) and 30 amps continuous. Each MOSFET has 2. 5 milliohms on-resistance.
Two are in the current path, so the loss is I to the 2R = 30² times 0. 005 = 4. 5 watts . A 1 milliohms shunt gives 30 millivolts and loses 30² times 0. 001 = 0. 9 watts.
An efficient switching regulator (a buck converter) makes the 5 volts supply, because a linear regulator, which burns the extra voltage as heat, would waste far more.
That is the whole idea: requirements first, then size each part with simple numbers.
"I'd clarify the spec first: say 4S, 30 amps continuous, 60 amps burst, DShot input, 5 volts BEC.

Architecture: sensorless six-step on a small MCU, three half-bridges of 40 volts low- R ds(on) MOSFETs, a three-phase gate driver with bootstrap and dead-time, back-EMF dividers, a low-side shunt and a buck BEC.
Sizing: about 7 watts total loss at 30 amps, bus capacitors for 15 amps ripple, 1 microfarads bootstrap.
Then firmware for startup and protections, and a test plan: double-pulse, thermal, desync, regen."
